title: Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.
lead: Peacock's subcontractors finished the job. The project owner went bankrupt without paying Peacock in full. The question was whether Peacock still had to pay the subcontractors.

actors.name: Peacock Construction Co.
actors.role: General contractor withholding final subcontract payments

actors.name: Modern Air Conditioning and Overly Manufacturing
actors.role: Subcontractors who completed the air-conditioning and rooftop-pool work

proceedings: Each subcontractor won summary judgment in the circuit court, meaning judgment without a trial.
The Second District Court of Appeal affirmed both judgments.
The Florida Supreme Court adopted those decisions and discharged its certiorari orders. Both judgments remained in place.
limits: This decision explains unclear final-payment clauses in subcontracts. A clearly written clause can still put the owner's nonpayment risk on the subcontractor. The court did not set a precise new payment date or decide how every contractual ambiguity must be resolved.

sections.title: The project’s owner does not pay in full
paragraphs: Peacock managed a condominium project as the general contractor. It hired Modern Air Conditioning for heating and air conditioning, and Overly Manufacturing for the rooftop swimming pool. Each subcontract made final payment due within thirty days after the work was complete, the architect accepted it in writing, and the owner paid in full.

Both subcontractors completed their work and asked for payment. No defects had been found. Modern's architect testified that the equipment met the plans and specifications, although it had not yet been operated.

The owner was a corporation that had entered bankruptcy. It had not paid Peacock in full. Peacock argued that it did not yet owe the subcontractors anything. The alternative reading was that Peacock still owed the money, but had a reasonable time to pay.

sections.title: Both subcontractors obtain summary judgment
sections.cue: A conflict concerns whether intent must go to a jury
paragraphs: Modern and Overly sued separately in Lee County Circuit Court. Each won summary judgment, without a trial. The Second District affirmed Modern's judgment: the clause was a promise to pay within a reasonable time, not a condition that could eliminate payment. It then affirmed Overly's judgment by following Modern's case.

The Florida Supreme Court accepted conflict certiorari, review to resolve a disagreement between Florida appeals courts, and considered the two cases together. In Gerrits, the Third District had sent a similar case to a jury to decide what the parties intended.

Peacock asked the Supreme Court to follow Gerrits. It accepted that most courts took the other view, but wanted to offer evidence of intent. Peacock argued that the judge should direct a verdict for the subcontractors only if no evidence supported making the owner's payment a condition.

sections.title: The familiar commercial relationship resolves the ambiguity
sections.cue: Clear language can allocate a different risk
paragraphs: Acting Chief Justice Boyd accepted that the wording could have either meaning. The court did not say Peacock's reading was impossible. But it rejected the idea that every ambiguity automatically required a jury. A judge could identify the ordinary intent behind this familiar business transaction as a question of law.

Small subcontractors need payment to stay in business. They do not ordinarily agree to absorb the risk that the project owner will never pay. The court therefore read unclear clauses of this kind as promises to pay within a reasonable time. Merely listing the owner's payment alongside completion and acceptance did not clearly transfer the risk of permanent nonpayment.
The parties could choose to shift that risk. But the contract had to express that intention clearly, and the general contractor bore the burden of making it clear. These contracts did not do so.

sections.title: The subcontractor judgments remain in effect
sections.cue: The conflicting precedent is displaced to that extent
paragraphs: On December 15, 1977, the Supreme Court adopted the Second District's decisions as controlling Florida law. It overruled Gerrits to the extent that decision conflicted, and discharged the orders allowing certiorari. Both judgments for the subcontractors remained in place. They did not depend on the bankrupt owner eventually paying Peacock.
Justices England, Sundberg, Hatchett, and Karl joined Boyd. No separate opinion was reported.
